slides.q: Will a raise bump me into a higher tax bracket?
slides.a: It might, but you won't take home less because of it. US income tax brackets are marginal, so only dollars above each threshold get taxed at the higher rate. The rest of your income is taxed the same as before. For income tax, a raise always leaves you with more money, even if a slice is taxed a bit higher.

slides.q: Can I negotiate a medical bill?
slides.a: Often, yes. Ask for an itemized bill and check it for errors or duplicate charges. Then call the billing office and ask about financial assistance, a cash discount, or a payment plan. Many hospitals, especially nonprofits, have charity care programs. Be polite and persistent, and get any agreement in writing before you pay.

slides.q: What's a cash advance on a credit card?
slides.a: It's borrowing cash against your credit card, like at an ATM. It's usually one of the priciest ways to borrow: there's typically an upfront fee, a higher interest rate than purchases, and interest starts right away with no grace period. Check your card's terms first, and look at cheaper options if you can.

A fiduciary is legally required to act in your best interest, not just recommend things that are 'suitable.' That matters because some advisors earn commissions on the products they sell you. A simple question to ask is 'Are you a fiduciary at all times?' Fee-only advisors, paid directly by you, generally avoid those commission conflicts.

slides.q: What's the difference between a pension and a 401(k)?
slides.a: A pension is run by your employer and promises a set monthly payment in retirement, usually based on your salary and years worked. A 401(k) is an account you contribute to, often with an employer match, and what you get depends on how much you save and how investments do. Pensions are much rarer at private companies today.
